content.text: Unit 1 Overview

Unit 1 is about how computing innovations are created — through collaboration, iterative design, careful documentation, and thorough testing. It covers four topics: Collaboration (1.1), Program Function and Purpose (1.2), Program Design and Development (1.3), and Identifying and Correcting Errors (1.4). This unit accounts for 10–13% of the AP exam. The central idea is that incorporating multiple perspectives through collaboration improves computing innovations, and that developers create better programs by using an iterative, user-focused development process.

content.label: Big Idea
content.text: Incorporating multiple perspectives through collaboration improves computing innovations as they are developed. Developers create and innovate using an iterative design process that is user-focused, incorporates implementation and feedback cycles, and leaves ample room for experimentation and risk-taking.
Topic 1.1 — Collaboration: What Is a Computing Innovation?

Before anything else, you need to be able to identify whether something is a computing innovation. The test is simple: does it require a program as an integral part of its function? If yes, it is a computing innovation. If it can function without any program at all, it is not.

content.definition: Any innovation that includes a program as an integral part of its function. Computing innovations can be physical (require hardware that runs a program), nonphysical computing software (standalone applications), or nonphysical computing concepts (systems or models enabled by computing).

rows: Physical
A tangible device that requires a program to function — without the program, it cannot work
Self-driving car, smart insulin pump, fitness tracker, smart thermostat, pacemaker with digital controls
Nonphysical Software
A standalone application or program that exists as software
Photo editing app, word processor, video game, navigation app, social media platform
Nonphysical Concept
A system, model, or way of doing things that only exists because of computing
E-commerce, online banking, ride-sharing services, streaming platforms, cloud storage

headers: NOT a Computing Innovation ✗ — no program needed
rows: Smart insulin pump — monitors blood sugar and doses insulin via a program
Mechanical clock — operates entirely through gears and springs
Ride-sharing platform — requires software to match drivers and riders
Printed cookbook — no program required to read and use it
Photo editing app — the program IS the innovation
Regular bicycle — no program needed to function
E-commerce website — buying and selling enabled by computing systems
Paper newspaper — no program required to read it
Smart thermostat — learns preferences and controls temperature via a program
Analog thermometer — measures temperature mechanically with no software

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: The exam often tests whether you can classify innovations correctly. A regular car is NOT a computing innovation. A self-driving car IS. A printed book is NOT. An e-reader IS. The key question: does it REQUIRE a program as an integral part of its function?
Topic 1.1 — Why Collaboration Improves Innovations

Effective collaboration produces a computing innovation that reflects the diversity of talents and perspectives of those who designed it. When team members come from different backgrounds and have different experiences, they catch each other's blind spots, identify needs that a single person would miss, and produce a better product overall.

Collaboration that includes diverse perspectives helps avoid bias in the development of computing innovations. Here is a concrete example: imagine a team building a voice recognition system consisting entirely of native English speakers from the same region. They test it thoroughly among themselves and it works great — for them. After release, they discover it performs poorly for users with accents, non-native speakers, and people with certain speech patterns. The team's lack of diversity meant they never encountered the system's failure modes for users unlike themselves. A more diverse team would have caught this in development.

content.label: Common Mistake
content.text: Collaboration is NOT the same as group work. Effective collaboration requires equal participation and voice from all members. In group work, some members may dominate while others barely contribute. In true collaboration, every perspective is valued and incorporated — this is what produces innovations that reflect the diversity of the team.

rows: Equal participation and voice from all members
Some members dominate, others barely contribute
Disagreements resolved through conflict resolution and negotiation
Disagreements avoided or suppressed by the loudest member
Final product reflects all members' perspectives
Final product reflects the strongest personality's preferences
Users from diverse backgrounds are consulted throughout
Only team members' own experiences are considered

content.text: Topic 1.1 — Collaboration Models and Tools

content.definition: A recognized collaboration model where one programmer writes code while another observes and provides real-time feedback. Both roles actively contribute — the observer catches errors the writer might miss. Roles are typically switched regularly so both programmers experience both perspectives.

rows: Writer (driver)
Types the code, focuses on implementing the current task one line at a time
Handles the immediate coding work and syntax
Observer (navigator)
Watches the code being written, points out errors, thinks ahead about the bigger picture
Catches mistakes in real time before they compound — actively contributes to the final product

content.text: Online tools support collaboration by allowing programmers to share and provide feedback on ideas and documents. These tools enable teams to work together regardless of physical location, share code, leave comments, track changes, review each other's contributions, and maintain a shared history of the project's development.
Topic 1.1 — The Four Interpersonal Skills

Effective collaborative teams practice specific interpersonal skills. These are different from technical programming skills — they govern how team members interact with each other to make the collaboration productive and equitable.

content.definition: Clearly and effectively sharing ideas, progress, concerns, and feedback with all team members so everyone stays informed, aligned, and able to contribute meaningfully.
Working toward an agreement that all team members can accept and support, even if it is not everyone's original preference. The goal is genuine alignment, not just majority rule.
Identifying and addressing disagreements within the team in a productive way that allows the project to move forward without lasting damage to team relationships or the quality of the work.

Working through differences in opinion, approach, or priorities to reach a compromise that satisfies the core needs of the team and the project without requiring any member to abandon their key concerns.

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: You must know exactly four interpersonal skills: communication, consensus building, conflict resolution, and negotiation. These are often confused with collaboration models (pair programming) or investigation methods (surveys, interviews). On the exam, be ready to classify each correctly.
Topic 1.1 — Gathering User Feedback

Consultation and communication with users are important aspects of the development of computing innovations. Information gathered from potential users can be used to understand the purpose of a program from diverse perspectives and to develop a program that fully incorporates those perspectives. User feedback is not optional — it is essential for building programs that actually meet real-world needs.

rows: Surveys
Collecting structured written responses from many users via questionnaires
Getting broad input from many users efficiently at scale
Interviews
One-on-one conversations with individual users asking open-ended questions
Getting in-depth qualitative perspectives and following up on specific answers
User testing
Watching users interact with the product and observing where they struggle or succeed
Identifying usability problems that users may not be able to verbalize in a survey
Direct observations
Watching how users currently perform the task before the program exists
Understanding the real problem and workflow before designing any solution

content.text: Topic 1.2 — Program Function and Purpose

The purpose of computing innovations is to solve problems or to pursue interests through creative expression. An understanding of the purpose of a computing innovation provides developers with an improved ability to develop that innovation — knowing WHY a program exists guides every design decision about HOW it is built.

content.definition: A collection of program statements that performs a specific task when run by a computer. A program is often referred to as software. A program needs to work for a variety of inputs and situations — not just the ones the developer tested.
A collection of program statements that is part of a program. A code segment does not perform a complete task independently — it is a piece of a larger program.
How a program functions during execution. Program behavior is often described by how a user interacts with it — what the user can do, what the program responds with, and the overall experience.

rows: A complete collection of statements that performs a specific task when run
A collection of statements that is part of a larger program
Can run independently and complete a task on its own
Cannot perform a complete task alone — it is a piece of the whole
Example: a weather app that takes a city name and displays the forecast
Example: the specific function inside the app that sends the request to the weather API

content.text: A program can be described at two levels of detail. A broad description covers what the program does — its inputs and outputs. A detailed description covers both what the program does AND how the program statements accomplish this. Both are valid ways to describe a program depending on the audience and context.

rows: Describes inputs and outputs at a high level
Describes inputs, outputs, AND the steps the program takes to get there
Appropriate for users who just need to know what the program does
Appropriate for other developers who need to understand and maintain the code
Example: 'The app takes a city name and displays the current weather'
Example: 'The app takes a city name string, constructs an API URL, sends an HTTP GET request, parses the JSON temperature field, converts Kelvin to Fahrenheit, and displays it on screen'

content.text: Topic 1.2 — Program Input

content.definition: Data sent to a computer for processing by a program. Input can come in a variety of forms — tactile, audio, visual, or text. Critically, input can come from a user OR from other programs.

rows: Tactile
Physical touch or button interactions
Screen tap, mouse click, keyboard press, controller button
Audio
Sound captured by the device
Voice command to a virtual assistant, microphone recording
Visual
Images or video captured by a camera
Photo taken for a filter app, QR code scanned, face for face recognition
Text
Characters typed or submitted
Search query typed, form filled out, message composed
From other programs
Data received from external software or services
Temperature data from a weather API, location from a GPS service, scores from another app

content.text: Topic 1.2 — Events and Event-Driven Programming

content.definition: An action that is associated with a trigger and supplies input data to a program. Events can be generated when a key is pressed, a mouse is clicked, a program is started, or any other defined action occurs that affects the flow of execution.

A programming style where program statements execute when triggered by an event rather than through the sequential flow of control. The program waits for events to occur and responds to them as they happen.

rows: Statements execute in order from top to bottom, one after another
Statements execute when triggered by an event — could be any time
The program runs through its statements once and completes
The program waits indefinitely, responding to events as users trigger them
Predictable, linear execution path
Execution path depends on what events occur and in what order
Example: a script that reads a file, processes it, and saves results
Example: a music app that responds to play, pause, skip, and volume buttons

items: Key pressed on keyboard → event triggered → program responds
Mouse clicked on a button → event triggered → program responds
Program first starts → event triggered → initialization code runs
Timer reaches zero → event triggered → countdown complete action runs
File finishes downloading → event triggered → success notification appears
User speaks a voice command → event triggered → virtual assistant processes speech

content.text: Topic 1.2 — Program Output

content.definition: Any data sent from a program to a device. Program output can come in a variety of forms — tactile, audio, visual, or text. Output is usually based on a program's input or its prior state (what it has previously computed or stored).

rows: Visual
Text displayed on screen, images rendered, videos played, charts drawn, maps shown
Audio
Sounds played, voice responses from assistants, music output, notification sounds
Tactile
Phone vibration, haptic feedback on a game controller, vibration alert
Text
Text messages sent, files written, data exported to a spreadsheet, emails sent

content.text: Inputs usually affect the output produced by a program. This input-process-output model is fundamental: data goes in, the program processes it, and results come out. The output is typically based on the current input or the program's prior state — what it has already computed, stored, or received before this moment.

rows: Weather app
City name typed by user
Fetches and parses weather data
Temperature and forecast shown on screen
Navigation app
Start and end locations entered
Calculates shortest route
Map with route displayed
Music streaming app
User taps play button (event)
Loads audio file from server
Song plays through speaker (audio output)
Fitness tracker
Steps counted by accelerometer
Adds to running daily total
Progress bar and step count displayed
Calculator
Numbers and operator entered
Performs arithmetic
Result displayed on screen

content.label: Common Mistake
content.text: Do not confuse input and output. INPUT is data going INTO the program for processing. OUTPUT is data coming OUT of the program to a device. The city name a user types is INPUT. The temperature displayed is OUTPUT. A button tap is an EVENT that provides INPUT. The updated screen is OUTPUT.
Topic 1.3 — The Development Process

Creating a program involves a full development process. A development process can be ordered and intentional, or exploratory in nature — there is no single correct approach. The following four phases are commonly used and you must know all of them.

rows: Investigating and reflecting
Understanding the problem, the users, constraints, and what the program needs to do
Surveys, interviews, user testing, direct observations, reviewing existing solutions
Designing
Planning how to accomplish the specification — what the program will look like and how it will be structured
Brainstorming, storyboarding, UI layout diagrams, organizing into modules, developing a testing strategy
Prototyping
Building an early working version of the program
Writing the first version of the code, creating a functional mockup, building a minimal viable product
Testing
Verifying that the program works correctly for all required inputs and situations
Running test cases, debugging, hand tracing, checking outputs against expected results

content.text: Topic 1.3 — Iterative vs Incremental Development

content.definition: A development process that requires refinement and revision based on feedback, testing, or reflection throughout the process. This may require revisiting earlier phases — for example, going back to redesign after testing reveals a fundamental problem.

A development process that breaks the problem into smaller pieces and makes sure each piece works before adding it to the whole. Each increment is built, verified, and integrated before the next begins.

rows: Refines and revises the program based on feedback throughout the process
Breaks the problem into pieces and verifies each before adding to the whole
May revisit earlier phases — the process is cyclical, not linear
Sequential piece by piece — one verified increment before the next begins
Driven by feedback, testing, and reflection at each cycle
Driven by completion and verification of each individual piece
Example: release app → users say interface is confusing → redesign → re-release → repeat
Example: build and fully test login system → then build and test profile page → then build and test feed

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: Iterative vs incremental is one of the most heavily tested concepts in Unit 1. Iterative = a team that releases, gets feedback, revises, and re-releases repeatedly. Incremental = a team that completes and verifies one piece before starting the next. A team can use BOTH approaches simultaneously.
Topic 1.3 — Investigation and Design

The design of a program incorporates investigation to determine its requirements. Investigation is useful for understanding and identifying the program constraints, as well as the concerns and interests of the people who will use the program. Investigation happens BEFORE design — you need to understand the problem before you can plan the solution.

content.definition: A description of how a program functions and may include a description of user interactions that a program must provide. Requirements define WHAT the program needs to do — not how it will do it.
The formal document that defines the requirements for the program. The design phase then outlines how to accomplish the given specification.

content.text: The design phase of a program may include: brainstorming, planning and storyboarding, organizing the program into modules and functional components, creation of diagrams that represent the layouts of the user interface, and development of a testing strategy for the program.

rows: Surveys — collecting structured feedback from many users
Brainstorming — generating ideas for how the program will work
Interviews — gathering in-depth perspectives from individual users
Storyboarding — mapping out the sequence and flow of the program
User testing — watching users interact with the product
Creating UI diagrams — sketching what screens and interfaces will look like
Direct observations — watching how users do the task today
Organizing into modules — breaking the program into manageable components
Identifying constraints and user concerns
Developing a testing strategy — planning how the program will be verified

content.text: Topic 1.3 — Documentation and Acknowledging Others

content.definition: A written description of the function of a code segment, event, procedure, or program and how it was developed. Documentation helps in developing and maintaining correct programs when working individually or in collaborative environments.

A form of program documentation written directly into the program to be read by people. Comments do NOT affect how a program runs — they are completely ignored by the computer. Programmers should document throughout development, not just at the end.

items: Programmers should document a program THROUGHOUT its development — not only at the end when everything is working
Documentation helps the original programmer remember decisions and helps other programmers understand the code
Not all programming environments support comments — in those cases, other methods of documentation are required
It is important to acknowledge any code segments that were developed collaboratively or by another source
Acknowledgement of code written by someone else goes in the program documentation
The acknowledgement must include the origin or original author's name — a vague mention is not sufficient

rows: You wrote all the code yourself
Document your own code with comments and descriptions throughout development
You developed code collaboratively with teammates
Acknowledge it in the program documentation, noting the collaborative development
You used code from an online source or textbook
Acknowledge it in documentation including the origin and original author's name
Your environment does not support comments
Use other documentation methods — external files, wikis, README documents, etc.

content.label: Common Mistake
content.text: Two big ones: (1) Comments do NOT affect how a program runs — do not confuse documentation with program logic. (2) Using someone else's code without acknowledgement is plagiarism even in programming. The acknowledgement must include the origin or author's name and goes in the program documentation.
Topic 1.4 — The Four Types of Errors

Errors are an inevitable part of programming. Knowing exactly what type of error you are dealing with is the first step toward fixing it. The four types have very distinct characteristics — learn to tell them apart.

content.definition: A mistake in the algorithm or program that causes it to behave incorrectly or unexpectedly. The program runs without crashing and produces no error messages — it simply gives wrong results. The algorithm itself is flawed.
A mistake in the program where the rules of the programming language are not followed. The program CANNOT run at all until the syntax error is corrected. It is caught before execution begins.

A mistake in the program that occurs during the execution of a program. The program starts running successfully but fails and crashes at a specific point during execution. Programming languages define their own run-time errors.

An error that occurs when a computer attempts to handle a number that is outside of the defined range of values. For example, storing 300 in a variable that can only hold values 0–255 causes an overflow error.

rows: Logic error
The algorithm is incorrectly designed
Yes — runs but gives wrong answers
Output is wrong but no error message
Program divides sum by 2 instead of 3 to find average of 3 numbers
Syntax error
Language rules are not followed
No — cannot run until fixed
Error message before program starts
Misspelled variable: rezult instead of result
Run-time error
During execution of the program
Starts, then crashes at the error line
Error message when the specific line executes
Dividing by zero when denominator variable is 0
Overflow error
A number exceeds the defined value range
May run, then give wrong result or crash
Unexpected wrong value or crash for large numbers
Revenue counter hits maximum integer value and wraps to negative

content.code:
Example — Logic Error:
score1 ← 85
score2 ← 90
score3 ← 78
total ← score1 + score2 + score3
average ← total / 2    ← LOGIC ERROR: should be / 3
DISPLAY average        ← displays 126.5 instead of the correct 84.33

The program runs perfectly. No crash. No error message.
But the algorithm is wrong — it divides by 2 instead of 3.

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: The most common confusion: logic error vs run-time error. A LOGIC ERROR runs without crashing but gives wrong answers. A RUN-TIME ERROR actually crashes the program during execution. If the program finishes running but the output is wrong → logic error. If the program crashes partway through → run-time error.
Topic 1.4 — Five Ways to Find and Correct Errors
The following five methods are all effective ways to find and correct errors. You must know all five for the exam and be able to identify which one is being used in a given scenario.

content.definition: Defined inputs used to check whether a program produces the expected output. A test case specifies both the input AND the expected output — if the actual output differs from the expected output, an error has been found.

Manually stepping through the code line by line on paper, tracking the value of each variable at each step. This allows a programmer to identify exactly where a variable takes on an unexpected value — ideal for finding logic errors in small code segments.
Using diagrams, flowcharts, or other visual representations of the program's execution to understand how it behaves and identify where the logic may be incorrect or incomplete.

A tool that allows programmers to pause execution at specific points (breakpoints), inspect the current values of all variables, and step through the code one line at a time. More powerful than adding output statements for complex programs.

Inserting temporary DISPLAY or print statements at key points in the code to show the values of variables during execution. Helps identify where values become incorrect by narrowing down the location of the error.

rows: Test cases
Run program with specific defined inputs and check actual output against expected output
Finding errors that only appear for certain inputs; systematic verification
Hand tracing
Manually track variable values through each line of code on paper
Logic errors in small or medium code segments where the algorithm is suspect
Visualizations
Create diagrams or flowcharts showing how the program executes
Understanding complex program structure and identifying logical gaps
Debugger
Use a tool to pause at breakpoints and inspect variable values
Larger programs where hand tracing is impractical; finding where values go wrong
Extra output statements
Insert temporary DISPLAY statements showing variable values at key points
Quick identification of approximately where values become incorrect

content.text: Topic 1.4 — Testing Strategy

In the development process, testing uses defined inputs to ensure that an algorithm or program is producing the expected outcomes. Programmers use the results from testing to revise their algorithms or programs. Testing is not a one-time event at the end of development — it is an ongoing activity throughout the process.

items: Defined inputs used to test a program should demonstrate the different expected outcomes that are at or just beyond the extremes (minimum and maximum) of input data
Testing at the boundaries catches the most common edge case errors — off-by-one mistakes, wrong comparisons, and boundary condition failures
Program requirements are needed to identify appropriate defined inputs for testing — you cannot write a test case without knowing what the correct output should be
The results from testing are used to revise algorithms and programs — testing drives improvement

rows: Program accepts ages 0–120
0 to 120 inclusive
0, 1, 119, 120, and invalid values -1 and 121
Tests exact minimum, just above minimum, just below maximum, exact maximum, and just outside both ends
Program accepts scores 0–100
0 to 100 inclusive
0, 1, 50, 99, 100, and invalid values -1 and 101
Covers minimum, just above minimum, middle, just below maximum, maximum, and both invalid extremes
Program averages a list of numbers
Any list length ≥ 1
List with one element, typical list, very large list, empty list
Tests edge cases including the empty list which might cause division by zero

content.label: Common Mistake
content.text: Students only test values in the middle of the valid range. The most important test inputs are AT and just BEYOND the extremes — minimum, maximum, one below minimum, one above maximum. These boundary values are where programs most commonly fail due to off-by-one errors and incorrect comparison operators.
Connecting the Topics: How Unit 1 Fits Together

The four topics in Unit 1 are deeply connected. Collaboration (1.1) shapes what gets built and for whom. Understanding program function and purpose (1.2) defines what inputs and outputs the program needs. The development process (1.3) provides the structure for building it — with investigation, design, prototyping, and testing phases. And identifying and correcting errors (1.4) is what makes the program actually work correctly through systematic testing and debugging.

rows: Who is building it and why?
1.1 Collaboration
Diverse team, pair programming, user consultation, interpersonal skills
What does it need to do?
1.2 Program Function and Purpose
Define purpose, identify inputs/outputs, understand program behavior
How will it be built?
1.3 Program Design and Development
Investigate → Design → Prototype → Test, with iterative or incremental approaches
Does it work correctly?
1.4 Identifying and Correcting Errors
Find logic/syntax/run-time/overflow errors using test cases, debuggers, hand tracing, etc.
